name: Chemistry Basics
author: Recurse
subject: science
description: Atoms, the periodic table, bonding, moles and stoichiometry, reaction energy and rates, equilibrium, acids and bases.

lesson.intro: Chemistry is the study of what matter is made of and how it changes. Everything is built from about a hundred kinds of atoms, and how an atom is put together decides how it bonds and reacts.
objectives: Work out the protons, neutrons and electrons in any atom, isotope or ion
Use the periodic table to predict valence electrons, reactivity and size
Predict whether a bond is ionic or covalent and explain its properties
Balance equations and use moles and mole ratios to calculate amounts
Explain reaction energy, rates, equilibrium and pH

sections.title: Inside the atom
sections.key: Protons set the element, neutrons set the isotope, and electrons set the charge; the mass number counts protons plus neutrons.
sections.body:
Every atom has a tiny, dense **nucleus** surrounded by electrons in shells.

[[visual]]

The **atomic number** (the number of protons) defines the element: every atom with 6 protons is carbon. The **mass number** is protons plus neutrons. **Isotopes** are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons: carbon-12 has 6 and carbon-14 has 8, but both react as carbon.

[[visual 2]]

A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons. Gain or lose electrons and it becomes an **ion**: sodium loses one to become Na⁺, chlorine gains one to become Cl⁻.

Electrons fill shells from the inside out: the first holds up to 2, the second up to 8. Sodium's 11 electrons sit 2, 8, 1, and that lone outer electron is easy to lose. Outer-shell electrons are called **valence electrons**.

visual.title: The three particles
rows: About 1/1836 of a proton: adds almost nothing

sections.tip: Protons decide the element, neutrons decide the isotope, and electrons decide the charge.
sections.pitfall: Counting electrons in the mass number. The mass number is protons plus neutrons only; electrons are too light to count.

check.question: An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons. What is its mass number?
check.explanation: The mass number counts the particles in the nucleus: 17 protons + 18 neutrons = 35. Electrons are not counted because their mass is tiny. With 17 protons, this atom is chlorine-35.

sections.title: The periodic table
sections.key: Elements in the same group share their number of valence electrons, so they behave alike; atoms shrink across a period and grow down a group.
sections.body:
The periodic table lists the elements in order of atomic number, laid out so that elements that behave alike line up.

- **Periods** are rows. Each step right adds a proton and an electron; each new period starts a new shell.
- **Groups** are columns. Main-group elements in one group share their number of **valence electrons**, so they react alike.
- **Metals** fill the left and middle, **nonmetals** the upper right, and **metalloids** such as silicon the staircase line between them.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Two trends follow. **Atomic radius** shrinks across a period, because each extra proton pulls the same shell tighter, and grows down a group, because each row adds a shell. **Electronegativity**, an atom's pull on shared electrons, does the opposite. Fluorine has the most.

[[visual 3]]

Most symbols come from English names (H, C, O), but some come from Latin:

[[visual 4]]

visual.title: Period 2, left to right
visual.caption: Main groups are 1, 2 and 13 to 18. Helium is the exception in group 18, with 2.

visual.title: Three families to know
rows: Soft metals that react vigorously with water

sections.tip: The group tells you how an element behaves; the period tells you how many electron shells it has.
sections.pitfall: Assuming neighbors in a row behave alike. Shared chemistry runs down the columns (groups), not across the rows.

check.question: Which element is most similar in its chemistry to sodium (Na)?
check.explanation: Potassium is in group 1 with sodium, so it also has one valence electron and reacts in a similar way. Magnesium is sodium's neighbor in the same period, but neighbors along a row behave differently; it is columns, not rows, that share chemistry.

sections.title: Ionic and covalent bonds
sections.key: Metals give electrons to nonmetals to form ionic bonds, nonmetals share electron pairs in covalent bonds, and weaker forces between molecules set boiling points.
sections.body:
Atoms bond because the bonded arrangement is more stable, usually because each atom ends up with a full outer shell: eight electrons for most atoms (the **octet rule**), two for hydrogen.

[[visual]]

Sharing is not always equal. Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so in water the shared electrons sit nearer the oxygen. The oxygen gets a slight negative charge and the hydrogens a slight positive one: a **polar covalent bond**.

**Intermolecular forces** are the much weaker attractions between molecules. Boiling water does not break any O-H bonds; it pulls whole H₂O molecules apart. Polar water molecules attract each other strongly through **hydrogen bonds**, so water boils at 100 °C while methane, a molecule of similar size, boils at about −162 °C.

items.title: Ionic
points: The metal gives electrons to the nonmetal
Na + Cl → Na⁺ Cl⁻: one electron moves
Opposite ions attract in a giant crystal lattice, not molecules
High melting points: table salt melts at 801 °C
Conducts when melted or dissolved, because the ions can move; not as a solid

items.title: Covalent
points: Water, H-O-H: one shared pair per bond
A double bond shares two pairs: O=C=O
Small molecules have low melting and boiling points

sections.tip: Metal plus nonmetal: think ionic, electrons transferred. Nonmetal plus nonmetal: think covalent, electrons shared.
sections.pitfall: Thinking boiling breaks covalent bonds. Boiling and melting separate whole molecules; the bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

check.question: Which pair of elements is most likely to form an ionic compound?
check.explanation: Magnesium is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal, so magnesium gives two electrons to oxygen, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions. Every other pair is two nonmetals, which share electrons in covalent bonds.

sections.title: The mole and balanced equations
sections.key: A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, and its mass in grams equals the formula mass; balance equations by changing coefficients, never subscripts.
sections.body:
Atoms are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count them in **moles**. One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles (**Avogadro's number**), whether atoms, molecules or electrons.

The **molar mass**, in g/mol, equals the atomic or formula mass: carbon is about 12.0 g/mol. For a compound, add up its atoms.

[[visual]]

In a reaction, atoms are rearranged but never created or destroyed, so a **balanced equation** has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. Change only the **coefficients**, the large numbers in front. Changing a subscript changes the substance: H₂O is water, but H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: How many moles in 36 g of water?
Balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O

steps.label: Count atoms on each side
steps.work:
left: 2 H, 2 O
right: 2 H, 1 O

steps.label: Fix oxygen: 2 in front of H₂O
Fix hydrogen: 2 in front of H₂

visual.result: `2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O`: 4 H and 2 O on each side

sections.tip: Balance one element at a time, and leave elements that appear on their own, such as O₂, until last.
sections.pitfall: Balancing by changing subscripts. Only coefficients may change; the subscripts define which substance it is.

check.question: Which of these equations for burning methane is balanced?
check.explanation: Count each element: 1 carbon on each side, 4 hydrogens on each side (CH₄ and 2H₂O), and 4 oxygens on each side (2O₂ on the left; 2 in CO₂ plus 2 in 2H₂O on the right). Each of the other options leaves hydrogen or oxygen unbalanced.

sections.title: Stoichiometry: amounts from equations
sections.key: The coefficients of a balanced equation are mole ratios, so every amount question goes mass to moles, through the ratio, and back to mass.
sections.body:
A recipe that calls for 2 eggs per cake tells you that 6 eggs make 3 cakes. A balanced equation is a recipe written in moles, and **stoichiometry** is reading it that way.

[[visual]]

The coefficients count particles, not grams: 2 g of hydrogen does not react with 1 g of oxygen.

[[visual 2]]

The **limiting reactant** runs out first and decides how much product forms; the other reactant is left in excess.

[[visual 3]]

**Concentration** is moles per liter (mol/L, often written M). 0.5 mol of salt in 2 L of solution is 0.5 / 2 = 0.25 mol/L. Convert milliliters to liters first: 500 mL is 0.5 L.

visual.title: Reading 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
visual.caption: Mole ratio 2 : 1 : 2. Mass is conserved: 4 g + 32 g = 36 g.

visual.title: How much water from 8 g of hydrogen?
Burn 4 mol of H₂ with only 1 mol of O₂

steps.label: O₂ needed for all the H₂ (2 : 1)

visual.result: 2 mol of water, with 2 mol of H₂ in excess

sections.pitfall: Using the coefficients as mass ratios. They count moles, which means particles; convert grams to moles before you use them.

check.question: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, how many moles of NH₃ can form from 6 mol of H₂, with plenty of N₂?
check.explanation: The ratio of H₂ to NH₃ is 3 : 2, so 6 mol of H₂ gives 6 × 2/3 = 4 mol of NH₃. 9 mol flips the ratio, and 6 mol ignores it.

sections.title: Reactions: types, energy, acids and bases
sections.key: Breaking bonds absorbs energy and forming bonds releases it; on the pH scale, below 7 is acidic and each step is a factor of 10.
sections.body:
Most reactions you will meet fit a few patterns:

[[visual]]

Every reaction involves energy. Breaking bonds always takes energy in, and forming bonds always gives energy out. Which one is bigger decides the type:

[[visual 2]]

An **acid** releases hydrogen ions (H⁺) in water, like hydrochloric acid, HCl. A **base** accepts H⁺ or releases hydroxide ions (OH⁻), like sodium hydroxide, NaOH. An acid and a base **neutralize** each other, forming a salt and water: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

[[visual 3]]

The **pH** scale is logarithmic: each step of 1 is a factor of 10 in H⁺ concentration. pH 3 has ten times the H⁺ of pH 4, and a hundred times that of pH 5.

visual.title: Five reaction types
rows: Two or more substances combine into one
An element takes another's place in a compound
A fuel burns in oxygen, making CO₂ and water

items.title: Exothermic
points: Forming the new bonds releases more than breaking the old ones took
Releases heat: the surroundings warm up

items.title: Endothermic
points: Breaking the bonds takes more than forming the new ones releases
Absorbs heat: the surroundings cool down

sections.tip: Breaking bonds always costs energy. A reaction gives out energy only because the new bonds it forms release more than that.
sections.pitfall: Reading pH as linear. pH 3 is not slightly more acidic than pH 4: it has ten times the H⁺ concentration.

check.question: Heating limestone drives the reaction CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What type of reaction is it?
check.explanation: One compound breaks down into two simpler substances, which is decomposition. Synthesis is the reverse, where substances combine into one, and combustion needs a fuel reacting with oxygen.

sections.title: Reaction rates and equilibrium
sections.key: Anything that makes successful collisions more frequent speeds a reaction up, and a disturbed equilibrium shifts to partly undo the change.
sections.body:
Why does food last longer in the fridge, and why can fine flour dust explode when a bag of flour cannot? Both come down to collisions.

**Collision theory**: particles react only when they collide with at least a minimum energy, the **activation energy**, and in a suitable orientation.

[[visual]]

Many reactions are **reversible**, written with ⇌. In a closed container the forward and reverse reactions end up running at the same rate: **dynamic equilibrium**. Both keep going, but the amounts of everything stay constant.

**Le Chatelier's principle**: a disturbed equilibrium shifts to partly undo the change. Take the Haber process, which makes ammonia for fertilizers:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: What speeds a reaction up
rows: Particles move faster, collide more often, and far more collisions have enough energy
Raise the concentration (or pressure, for gases)
More particles in the same space: more collisions
Far more surface exposed, which is why fine dust can burn explosively
Offers a pathway with lower activation energy and is not used up. Enzymes are biological catalysts
visual.caption: The reverse slows a reaction: cooling (a fridge) or diluting with water.

visual.title: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (forward reaction exothermic)
rows: Uses up some of the added N₂

sections.deeper:
**Why ammonia plants run hot anyway.** Raising the temperature lowers the yield of NH₃, but at low temperatures the reaction is far too slow. Plants run at around 400 to 450 °C with an iron catalyst: a compromise between yield and rate.

A car's **catalytic converter** uses platinum-group metals to speed up reactions that clean up exhaust gases.
sections.pitfall: Thinking a catalyst increases how much product you get at equilibrium. It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium arrives sooner, but its position does not change.

check.question: Which change does NOT speed up a reaction?
choices: Crushing a solid reactant into a powder
Diluting the reactants with more water
check.explanation: Diluting lowers the concentration, so particles collide less often and the reaction slows down. The other three all raise the number of successful collisions per second.

keyTerms.definition: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus. It defines which element the atom is.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14.
An atom or group of atoms with an electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons.
Electrons in the outermost shell. They take part in bonding and set an element's chemistry.
A bond in which two atoms share a pair of electrons, typically between nonmetals.
An amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
A scale of acidity: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is basic. Each unit is a factor of 10.
Describes a reaction that releases energy, usually as heat, to its surroundings.
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams per mole, found by adding up the atomic masses in its formula.
The reactant that runs out first and so sets the maximum amount of product.
A substance that speeds up a reaction by lowering its activation energy, without being used up.
The state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse rates are equal, so amounts stay constant while both reactions continue.

summary: Protons set the element, neutrons the isotope, and electrons the charge.
A group shares its valence electrons and behavior; atoms shrink across a period and grow down a group.
Metal plus nonmetal: ionic, electrons transferred. Nonmetals: covalent, electrons shared.
moles = mass / molar mass; balance with coefficients, never subscripts.
Heat, concentration, surface area and catalysts speed reactions; a disturbed equilibrium shifts to undo the change.
Breaking bonds absorbs energy, forming them releases it; each pH step is a factor of 10.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why table salt forms hard crystals and conducts electricity when dissolved, while sugar dissolves without conducting, using what you know about ionic and covalent bonds.

questions.question: What determines which element an atom is?
questions.explanation: The atomic number, the count of protons, defines the element. Changing the number of neutrons gives a different isotope of the same element, and changing the number of electrons gives an ion, but neither changes the element.

questions.question: How many neutrons are in an atom of iron-56? Iron's atomic number is 26.
questions.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = 56 − 26 = 30. The atomic number gives the protons, and the number in the isotope's name is the mass number.

questions.question: A sodium atom turns into a sodium ion, Na⁺. What happened?
questions.explanation: Losing one negative electron leaves 11 protons and 10 electrons, so the ion has a +1 charge. Gaining a proton is the tempting answer, but protons never change in a chemical reaction; if they did, the atom would become a different element.

questions.question: Moving from sodium to argon across period 3, what happens to the size of the atoms?
questions.explanation: Each step adds a proton, while the new electrons go into the same outer shell. The stronger pull of the nucleus draws that shell in, so atoms shrink across a period. It is tempting to think more particles means a bigger atom, but size only jumps when a new shell starts in the next period.

questions.question: Why are noble gases such as neon and argon so unreactive?
choices: Their atoms are too heavy to move
Their outer electron shells are already full
questions.explanation: A full outer shell is already stable, so noble gas atoms gain nothing by gaining, losing or sharing electrons. They do have electrons and neutrons; argon, for example, has 18 electrons and 22 neutrons in its most common isotope.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for potassium?
questions.explanation: Potassium's symbol, K, comes from its Latin name, kalium. P is phosphorus and Po is polonium, so guessing from the English name does not work for this element.

questions.question: Compare ionic and covalent bonding: which kinds of elements form each, and what happens to the electrons?
questions.answer: Ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal: the metal transfers electrons to the nonmetal, and the oppositely charged ions attract. Covalent bonds form between nonmetals, which share pairs of electrons.
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is ionic; water (H₂O) and methane (CH₄) are covalent. The bond type explains properties: ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct when dissolved, while small covalent molecules usually do neither.

questions.question: Solid table salt does not conduct electricity, but salt dissolved in water does. Why?
choices: Dissolved ions are free to move and carry charge
Water supplies free electrons to the salt
Dissolving turns the ionic bonds into covalent bonds
Solid salt contains no charged particles
questions.explanation: Salt is made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in both forms. In the solid they are locked in place in a lattice; in water they separate and move, so they can carry a current. Solid salt is full of charged particles; they just cannot move.

questions.question: What is the molar mass of carbon dioxide, CO₂, in g/mol? Use C = 12 and O = 16.
questions.explanation: Add up the atoms: one carbon and two oxygens, 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 g/mol. A common slip is to count oxygen only once and get 28.

questions.question: How many moles are in 90 g of water? The molar mass of water is 18 g/mol.
questions.explanation: moles = mass / molar mass = 90 / 18 = 5 mol. A quick sanity check: 90 g is several times 18 g, so the answer must be several moles, not a fraction of a mole or a huge number.

questions.question: Fill in the missing coefficient to balance the equation: N₂ + 3H₂ → ? NH₃
questions.explanation: The left side has 2 nitrogen atoms and 6 hydrogen atoms. Two molecules of NH₃ also contain 2 nitrogens and 6 hydrogens, so 2 balances both elements: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.

questions.question: A student balances Na + Cl₂ → NaCl by rewriting it as Na + Cl₂ → NaCl₂. What is wrong?
choices: Nothing, because both sides now have two chlorine atoms
Changing a subscript makes a different formula; it should be 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl
Chlorine should be written as Cl, not Cl₂
The sodium should be changed to Na₂ instead
questions.explanation: Subscripts are part of a substance's identity. Sodium chloride is always NaCl, so balancing must use coefficients: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl has 2 sodium and 2 chlorine atoms on each side. Writing chlorine as Cl is also wrong, because chlorine gas exists as Cl₂ molecules.

questions.question: Vinegar has a pH of about 3, and pure water has a pH of 7. How many times greater is the H⁺ concentration in vinegar?
questions.explanation: The pH scale is logarithmic, so each step is a factor of 10. A difference of 4 steps is 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10,000. Treating the scale as linear and answering 4 is the most common mistake.

questions.question: As a reaction runs, its beaker gets noticeably warmer. What does this tell you?
choices: It is exothermic, releasing energy to the surroundings
Bonds are breaking but none are forming
questions.explanation: A reaction that warms its surroundings is giving out energy, so it is exothermic. An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings, so the beaker would feel cold instead.

questions.question: Which statement about chemical bonds and energy is correct?
choices: Breaking bonds releases energy, and forming bonds absorbs it
Both breaking and forming bonds release energy
Breaking and forming bonds involve no energy change
Breaking bonds absorbs energy, and forming bonds releases it
questions.explanation: Pulling bonded atoms apart always takes energy, and atoms give out energy when they bond. A reaction is exothermic overall only when its new bonds release more energy than breaking the old ones took. The idea that breaking bonds releases energy, often heard about fuels and food, is a common misconception.

questions.question: What type of reaction is Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂?
questions.explanation: Zinc, an element, takes the place of hydrogen in HCl, pushing the hydrogen out as H₂ gas. Swapping one element for another in a compound is single replacement. It is not synthesis, because two products form rather than one.

questions.question: What happens when an acid reacts with a base? Give an example.
questions.answer: The acid and base neutralize each other, forming a salt and water: H⁺ from the acid and OH⁻ from the base combine to make H₂O. For example, HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
questions.explanation: Neutralization is why antacid tablets, which are mild bases, relieve excess stomach acid. When a strong acid and a strong base react in exactly matching amounts, the resulting solution is neutral, at pH 7.

questions.question: Match each chemical symbol to its element.
questions.explanation: All six symbols come from Latin names: natrium, kalium, ferrum, argentum, plumbum and aurum. That is why they do not match the English names.

questions.question: Match each reaction to its type.
questions.explanation: Synthesis combines into one product, decomposition splits one reactant, single replacement swaps an element into a compound, double replacement swaps partners between two compounds, and combustion burns a fuel in oxygen to give CO₂ and water.

questions.question: How many electrons does a Mg²⁺ ion have? Magnesium's atomic number is 12.
questions.explanation: A neutral magnesium atom has 12 electrons. The 2+ charge means it lost two, leaving 10. Adding two (to get 14) would make a negative ion.

questions.question: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many grams of water form when 4 g of hydrogen gas burns completely? Use H = 1 and O = 16.
questions.explanation: 4 g of H₂ at 2 g/mol is 2 mol. The ratio H₂ : H₂O is 2 : 2, so 2 mol of water forms, and 2 × 18 = 36 g.

questions.question: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, you react 3 mol of H₂ with 2 mol of O₂. Which reactant is limiting, and how much water forms?
choices: O₂ is limiting, and 4 mol of water forms
H₂ is limiting, and 3 mol of water forms
O₂ is limiting, and 2 mol of water forms
Neither is limiting, and 5 mol of water forms
questions.explanation: 3 mol of H₂ needs only 1.5 mol of O₂, and 2 mol is available, so hydrogen runs out first. It makes 3 mol of water (ratio 2 : 2), leaving 0.5 mol of O₂ unused. 4 mol of water would need 4 mol of H₂.

questions.question: 0.5 mol of sugar is dissolved to make 250 mL of solution. What is the concentration, in mol/L?
questions.explanation: Convert the volume to liters first: 250 mL = 0.25 L. Then 0.5 mol / 0.25 L = 2 mol/L. Dividing by 250 without converting gives 0.002, which is far too small.

questions.question: Marble chips react with hydrochloric acid. Select every change that would speed up the reaction.
choices: Using marble powder instead of chips
Adding water to dilute the acid
Using a bigger beaker with the same contents
questions.explanation: Powder raises the surface area, warming raises collision energy and frequency, and stronger acid raises concentration. Diluting slows the reaction, and a bigger beaker changes nothing about how often particles collide.

questions.question: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is at equilibrium in a closed container. What happens if the pressure is increased?
choices: The equilibrium shifts left, because pressure favors reactants
Nothing, because pressure only changes the rate
The reaction stops until the pressure falls
The equilibrium shifts right, producing more NH₃
questions.explanation: By Le Chatelier's principle the system shifts to reduce the pressure, toward the side with fewer gas molecules. The right side has 2 molecules and the left has 4, so more NH₃ forms. Both reactions keep running; equilibrium is dynamic.

questions.question: What does a catalyst do?
choices: It is used up to supply energy to the reaction
It lowers the activation energy, so the reaction runs faster
It changes which products the reaction makes
It raises the temperature of the reactants
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an easier pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed. It comes out of the reaction unchanged, and it does not alter the products or heat anything up.

questions.question: Water (H₂O) boils at 100 °C, but methane (CH₄), a molecule of similar size, boils at about −162 °C. Why?
choices: Boiling water breaks its strong O–H bonds
Water molecules are much heavier than methane molecules
Polar water molecules attract each other strongly through hydrogen bonds
questions.explanation: Boiling separates molecules from each other, so what matters is the attraction between molecules. Water's polar molecules hold on to each other through hydrogen bonds; nonpolar methane molecules barely attract. The masses are similar (18 versus 16), and no bonds inside the molecules break.

questions.question: Put the steps for finding the mass of product from a known mass of reactant in order.
items: Convert the known mass to moles
Use the coefficients to find moles of product
Convert moles of product to grams
questions.explanation: The coefficients only make sense in moles, so you need a balanced equation and a mass-to-moles conversion before using them, and a moles-to-mass conversion at the end.

questions.question: Chlorine's 17 electrons are arranged in shells as 2, 8, 7. How many valence electrons does it have?
questions.explanation: Valence electrons are the ones in the outermost shell: 7. That matches chlorine's place in group 17, and it is one short of a full octet, so chlorine readily gains an electron to form Cl⁻.
